B.text: The earth fault loop is a series path, so its resistances add: Zs = Ze + (R1 + R2). Here R1 + R2 = 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.1 Ω, and adding Ze gives 0.2 + 1.1 = 1.3 Ω.

C.text: 0.22 Ω equals Ze × (R1 + R2), that is 0.2 × 1.1; values in series are added, not multiplied, so this is far below the 1.1 Ω of the circuit conductors.

D.text: 0.18 Ω is lower than the 0.6 Ω of the cpc on its own, which is impossible because Zs must always exceed both Ze and R1 + R2 individually.

questions.prompt: Under Regulation 14 of the Electricity at Work Regulations, which activity can be justified on or near live conductors, provided suitable precautions are taken?

options.A: Replacing a cracked socket-outlet on an energised circuit because the shop is open for trading
options.B: Connecting a new circuit into an energised consumer unit to avoid interrupting the occupier's supply
options.C: Measuring earth fault loop impedance at a socket-outlet, a test that needs the supply connected
options.D: Tightening a loose termination in an energised distribution board to save a return visit

questions.explanation: Regulation 14 permits work on or near a live conductor only when three conditions are all met: making it dead would be unreasonable, it is reasonable for the person to be working there while it is live, and suitable precautions against injury are in place. An earth fault loop impedance measurement relies on the supply voltage, so it cannot be carried out with the circuit dead, whereas repair and installation work can wait until the circuit has been safely isolated.

A.text: Replacing an accessory is repair work that can be done after safe isolation; keeping a shop trading does not make it unreasonable for the circuit to be dead.

B.text: Installation work inside a consumer unit does not need the supply present, so inconvenience to the occupier is no justification for leaving the busbars energised.

C.text: Regulation 14 permits work on or near a live conductor only when three conditions are all met: making it dead would be unreasonable, it is reasonable for the person to be working there while it is live, and suitable precautions against injury are in place. An earth fault loop impedance measurement relies on the supply voltage, so it cannot be carried out with the circuit dead, whereas repair and installation work can wait until the circuit has been safely isolated.

D.text: Saving a return visit does not make it unreasonable for the board to be dead; the termination should be tightened with the board isolated, even if that means coming back.

questions.prompt: Test equipment, leads and probes carry an installation overvoltage category (CAT) marking. Which location calls for CAT IV equipment rather than CAT III?

options.A: A socket-outlet on a ring final circuit
options.B: A sub-distribution board on an upper floor
options.C: The flex of a plug-connected appliance
options.D: The electricity meter at the origin

questions.explanation: CAT IV covers equipment at or near the origin, between the building entrance and the consumer unit, such as the electricity meter and the primary overcurrent protective devices. CAT III is sufficient for parts of the building wiring further downstream, including distribution boards and socket-outlets, while CAT II relates to equipment supplied from that wiring.

A.text: Socket-outlets form part of the building wiring installation, which is the zone CAT III equipment is intended for, so CAT IV is not needed there.

B.text: Distribution boards are named as CAT III locations; only the stretch between the building entrance and the primary board is treated as CAT IV.

C.text: Plug-connected equipment supplied from the building wiring falls in CAT II, the least onerous of the three markings described.

D.text: CAT IV covers equipment at or near the origin, between the building entrance and the consumer unit, such as the electricity meter and the primary overcurrent protective devices. CAT III is sufficient for parts of the building wiring further downstream, including distribution boards and socket-outlets, while CAT II relates to equipment supplied from that wiring.

questions.prompt: A test arrangement is made up of an instrument, leads, probes and connectors that carry different CAT markings. Which statement describes the equivalent overvoltage category of the complete arrangement?

options.A: It is the lowest category of any item connected in the arrangement
options.B: It is the category marked on the test instrument itself
options.C: It is the highest category of any item connected in the arrangement
options.D: It is the category of the test leads, since they carry the test current

questions.explanation: A test arrangement is only as well protected against transient overvoltages as its weakest component. Fitting CAT II probes or leads to a CAT IV instrument therefore reduces the whole set-up to CAT II, so every item must be rated for the location where it is to be used.

A.text: A test arrangement is only as well protected against transient overvoltages as its weakest component. Fitting CAT II probes or leads to a CAT IV instrument therefore reduces the whole set-up to CAT II, so every item must be rated for the location where it is to be used.

B.text: The instrument's marking covers the instrument only; leads, probes and connectors with a lesser marking would still be exposed to the same transients.

C.text: Taking the highest marking would let one well-rated item mask weaker ones, which is the opposite of how the equivalent category is assessed.

D.text: Leads are just one of the items counted; an instrument or probe with a lower marking than the leads would still set the limit.

questions.prompt: Particular attention to safety is needed when a test instrument can generate a test voltage above certain values. Which values apply in wet or damp conditions?
questions.explanation: For dry conditions the thresholds are 50 V AC or 120 V DC; where conditions are wet or damp they drop to half, 25 V AC or 60 V DC, reflecting the greater shock risk. Instruments that can exceed these values, such as insulation resistance testers, call for particular attention to safe working.

A.text: 50 V AC or 120 V DC are the thresholds given for dry conditions; they are too high to use where the surroundings are wet or damp.

B.text: For dry conditions the thresholds are 50 V AC or 120 V DC; where conditions are wet or damp they drop to half, 25 V AC or 60 V DC, reflecting the greater shock risk. Instruments that can exceed these values, such as insulation resistance testers, call for particular attention to safe working.

C.text: 12 V AC or 30 V DC is the limit up to which SELV or PELV circuits in wet areas generally need no insulation for basic protection (Regulation 414.4.5); it is not the test-voltage threshold given for wet or damp conditions.

D.text: This pairs the wet-condition AC figure with the dry-condition DC figure; in wet or damp conditions the DC threshold also halves, to 60 V.

questions.prompt: What action should the inspector take, both before and after testing, to confirm isolation of the supply?

options.A: Attach a warning label at the isolator stating 'do not switch on'
options.B: Confirm the operation of the approved voltage indicator
options.C: Lock the main switch in the open position
options.D: Switch the main isolator on and off

questions.explanation: The safe isolation procedure requires proving the tester works before and after checking the circuit. This ensures that the voltage indicator did not fail during the process, preventing a dangerous false 'dead' reading.

A.text: A notice helps prevent interference but cannot show that the detector remained functional during the absence-of-voltage check. The indicator needs a known source before and after use.

B.text: The safe isolation procedure requires proving the tester works before and after checking the circuit. This ensures that the voltage indicator did not fail during the process, preventing a dangerous false 'dead' reading.

C.text: Locking off secures the disconnection and is an essential separate step. It does not prove the test instrument, so it cannot guard against a false dead indication caused by instrument failure.

D.text: Operating the isolator neither proves every relevant conductor dead nor verifies the detector. Re-energising during the process would also defeat the secured safe-isolation state.

questions.prompt: GS38 recommends that suitable high breaking capacity (HBC) fuses, or another means of limiting current, are provided in test leads or test equipment. What is this measure intended to achieve?

options.A: Reduce the risks from accidental contact and from arcing under fault conditions
options.B: Improve the accuracy of low-resistance readings by stabilising the test current
options.C: Allow live measurements where no overcurrent protection exists upstream of the test point
options.D: Raise the overvoltage category of the leads to match that of the instrument

questions.explanation: If a probe slips and bridges live parts, or a lead or instrument fails, a very large fault current can flow and produce a dangerous arc. A high breaking capacity fuse or other current-limiting device in the lead or instrument restricts that energy, lowering the danger from inadvertent contact and from arcing.

A.text: If a probe slips and bridges live parts, or a lead or instrument fails, a very large fault current can flow and produce a dangerous arc. A high breaking capacity fuse or other current-limiting device in the lead or instrument restricts that energy, lowering the danger from inadvertent contact and from arcing.

B.text: Fused leads add resistance and are listed among the causes of measurement error, so they do nothing to improve the accuracy of readings.

C.text: Fused leads alone do not make up for missing overcurrent protection between the test point and the supply transformer; a suitably rated device must be present or temporarily fitted.

D.text: A fuse does not change a CAT marking; the arrangement still takes the lowest category of any lead, probe or instrument connected in it.

questions.prompt: Some instrument manufacturers advise the use of non-fused leads and probes because the instrument has in-built electrical protection. What should the inspector note about that in-built protection?

options.A: It makes the GS38 precautions unnecessary for the leads
options.B: It also covers leads supplied by the instrument manufacturer
options.C: It does not extend to the probes and leads
options.D: It gives the leads the same overvoltage category as the instrument

questions.explanation: Protection built into an instrument sits inside its case, so a damaged lead, or a probe bridging live parts, is on the supply side of that protection and is not limited by it. The GS38 precautions still apply to all leads, probes and accessories, and a risk assessment should decide whether fused leads are needed where there is doubt.

A.text: GS38 precautions are to be observed for all instruments, leads, probes and accessories, whatever protection the instrument itself contains.

B.text: Leads from the instrument's own manufacturer are no exception; the limitation is stated without qualification, so, whoever made the leads, they stay outside the internal protection.

C.text: Protection built into an instrument sits inside its case, so a damaged lead, or a probe bridging live parts, is on the supply side of that protection and is not limited by it. The GS38 precautions still apply to all leads, probes and accessories, and a risk assessment should decide whether fused leads are needed where there is doubt.

D.text: Category markings belong to each item separately and the complete arrangement takes the lowest of them; internal protection cannot upgrade a lead.

questions.prompt: BS 7671 defines verification as all measures by means of which compliance of the electrical installation with the relevant requirements is checked. Which three activities does this definition comprise?
questions.explanation: In BS 7671, verification covers every measure used to check that an installation meets the relevant requirements, and it is made up of three parts: inspection, testing and certification. The work is therefore not finished once readings have been taken, because the results must also be certified.

A.text: Design and construction are signed for separately on the Electrical Installation Certificate as the work being verified, and this list leaves out both testing and certification.

B.text: In BS 7671, verification covers every measure used to check that an installation meets the relevant requirements, and it is made up of three parts: inspection, testing and certification. The work is therefore not finished once readings have been taken, because the results must also be certified.

C.text: Design is a stage whose compliance is checked, not a means of checking it, and this combination drops inspection, which is one of the three parts.

D.text: Safe isolation is a precaution taken before dead working and not a compliance check, and this list omits inspection altogether.

questions.prompt: Regulation 641.2 requires information on the assessed general characteristics of an installation to be made available to the person carrying out the inspection and testing. Which of the following is NOT part of that information?

options.A: The maximum demand after diversity has been taken into account
options.B: The prospective short-circuit current at the origin of the installation
options.C: The type and rating of the overcurrent protective device at the origin
options.D: The measured R1 + R2 value of each final circuit

questions.explanation: The general characteristics handed to the inspector are the maximum demand, the number and type of live conductors, the earthing system, the nominal voltage, the nature of current and frequency, the prospective short-circuit current at the origin, Ze and the overcurrent device at the origin. R1 + R2 values are obtained by the inspector through continuity testing, so they are a result of verification and not information supplied beforehand.

A.text: Maximum demand, expressed in amps, kW or kVA after diversity, is the first listed characteristic (Regulation 311.1) and must be given to the inspector.

B.text: The prospective short-circuit current at the origin is one of the listed supply characteristics that the inspector is entitled to receive before starting.

C.text: The type and rating of the overcurrent protective device acting at the origin is the final item in the list of general characteristics to be provided.

D.text: The general characteristics handed to the inspector are the maximum demand, the number and type of live conductors, the earthing system, the nominal voltage, the nature of current and frequency, the prospective short-circuit current at the origin, Ze and the overcurrent device at the origin. R1 + R2 values are obtained by the inspector through continuity testing, so they are a result of verification and not information supplied beforehand.

questions.prompt: During initial verification an inspector needs to confirm that the installed cables are of the sizes selected by the designer. Which approach is the inspector reasonably expected to take?

options.A: Compare the installed sizes at the distribution board with the designer's cable schedule
options.B: Repeat the cable sizing calculations for every circuit and resize any cable found too small
options.C: Trace every cable along its whole route to prove the size is maintained throughout its length
options.D: Rely on the designer's signature on the certificate and make no check of cable sizes at all

questions.explanation: The inspector's checks exist only to confirm the work of others, so the reasonable method is to obtain the design information, such as a cable or circuit schedule, and compare it by visual inspection with what has been installed. The distribution board housing the circuits' protective devices is the most logical place to make that comparison.

A.text: The inspector's checks exist only to confirm the work of others, so the reasonable method is to obtain the design information, such as a cable or circuit schedule, and compare it by visual inspection with what has been installed. The distribution board housing the circuits' protective devices is the most logical place to make that comparison.

B.text: Design cable sizing checks remain the designer's responsibility, and the inspector is not meant to take over that duty or to fix the problems found.

C.text: Making sure a cable size is maintained along its full length is the duty of the installer or constructor, and it would be unreasonable to expect it of the inspector.

D.text: The inspector is still responsible for verifying aspects of both design and construction, so a visual comparison against the design information has to be made.

questions.prompt: During first-fix inspection of a new installation, a thermoplastic flat twin-and-earth cable is found buried 30 mm deep in a masonry wall, running vertically above a socket-outlet within the prescribed zone. It has no earthed metallic covering, no earthed containment and no mechanical protection, and it is not a SELV or PELV circuit. What must be provided for this cable?

options.A: No further measure, because a cable run within a prescribed zone needs nothing more
options.B: Fault protection by an RCD with a rated residual operating current not exceeding 300 mA
options.C: Additional protection by an RCD with a rated residual operating current not exceeding 30 mA
options.D: A warning notice at the consumer unit showing the route of the concealed cable

questions.explanation: Section 522.6 of BS 7671 treats a cable buried less than 50 mm into a wall or partition as vulnerable to nails and screws. Unless it has an earthed metallic covering, earthed containment, adequate mechanical protection or a SELV or PELV supply, an RCD with IΔn of 30 mA or less must give additional protection. Keeping the run inside the prescribed zones does not remove that requirement.

A.text: Prescribed zones only make the cable route predictable; a cable shallower than 50 mm still needs one of the listed protective methods even when it stays inside a zone.

B.text: A 300 mA device is too insensitive to count as additional protection; the limit set for a shallow concealed cable is a rated residual operating current of 30 mA.

C.text: Section 522.6 of BS 7671 treats a cable buried less than 50 mm into a wall or partition as vulnerable to nails and screws. Unless it has an earthed metallic covering, earthed containment, adequate mechanical protection or a SELV or PELV supply, an RCD with IΔn of 30 mA or less must give additional protection. Keeping the run inside the prescribed zones does not remove that requirement.

D.text: No such notice is called for, and a label cannot stop a nail or screw piercing the cable; the remedy has to be a protective measure applied to the circuit itself.

questions.prompt: BS 7671 requires arc fault detection devices (AFDDs) on single-phase AC circuits supplying socket-outlets rated up to 32 A in certain premises. In which of the following installations are they a requirement rather than a recommendation?
questions.explanation: Regulation 421.1.7 makes AFDDs mandatory for socket-outlet circuits up to 32 A in four kinds of premises: higher risk residential buildings, houses in multiple occupation, purpose-built student accommodation and care homes. Everywhere else they are only recommended and the decision rests with the designer, so an inspector cannot comment on their absence.

A.text: Regulation 421.1.7 makes AFDDs mandatory for socket-outlet circuits up to 32 A in four kinds of premises: higher risk residential buildings, houses in multiple occupation, purpose-built student accommodation and care homes. Everywhere else they are only recommended and the decision rests with the designer, so an inspector cannot comment on their absence.

B.text: A single-household dwelling is not one of the four listed premises, so AFDDs there are a recommendation that the designer may or may not adopt.

C.text: A shop is not residential accommodation of any kind, whereas all four listed premises are places where people live; here the designer simply chooses whether to fit AFDDs.

D.text: A commercial office does not appear among the premises named in Regulation 421.1.7, so fitting AFDDs there remains optional guidance only.

questions.prompt: When inspecting the conductors of a new three-phase AC distribution circuit, which colours should identify lines L1, L2 and L3 respectively?
questions.explanation: Under the harmonised identification scheme for AC power circuits, line 1 of a three-phase circuit is brown, line 2 is black and line 3 is grey, with blue kept for the neutral. Checking a representative sample of conductors against these colours, particularly at switchgear, forms part of the initial inspection.

A.text: These are the pre-harmonisation phase colours; under the current scheme blue marks the neutral, so it cannot be used to identify L3.

B.text: The right three colours appear but the last two are transposed: black belongs to L2 and grey to L3, not the other way round.

C.text: Brown identifies L1 and black identifies L2, so swapping the first two colours mislabels both of those lines even though grey is correct for L3.

D.text: Under the harmonised identification scheme for AC power circuits, line 1 of a three-phase circuit is brown, line 2 is black and line 3 is grey, with blue kept for the neutral. Checking a representative sample of conductors against these colours, particularly at switchgear, forms part of the initial inspection.

questions.prompt: Barriers and enclosures that provide basic protection are checked during initial inspection. Which statement gives the minimum degrees of protection they must provide?

options.A: IPXXA generally, and IPXXB or IP2X for a readily accessible horizontal top surface
options.B: IPXXB or IP2X generally, and IPXXD or IP4X for a readily accessible horizontal top surface
options.C: IPXXD or IP4X generally, and IPXXB or IP2X for a readily accessible horizontal top surface
options.D: IPX2 generally, and IPX4 for a readily accessible horizontal top surface

questions.explanation: Regulation 416.2 calls for barriers and enclosures to give at least IPXXB or IP2X, which prevents a finger reaching live parts. A horizontal top surface that is readily accessible must meet the tighter IPXXD or IP4X, because small objects or wires could otherwise fall or be pushed in from above.

A.text: IPXXA only guards against contact by the back of the hand, a lower level than the finger-proof IPXXB that is demanded as the general minimum.

B.text: Regulation 416.2 calls for barriers and enclosures to give at least IPXXB or IP2X, which prevents a finger reaching live parts. A horizontal top surface that is readily accessible must meet the tighter IPXXD or IP4X, because small objects or wires could otherwise fall or be pushed in from above.

C.text: The two requirements are reversed here: the stricter IPXXD or IP4X applies to the accessible top surface, not to every face of the enclosure.

D.text: The second characteristic numeral describes resistance to water ingress rather than access to live parts, so IPX2 and IPX4 are not the codes set for basic protection.

questions.prompt: During initial inspection some of the RCDs are found to be marked Type AC. For which application does BS 7671 permit a Type AC RCD to be used?

options.A: Fixed equipment where the load current is known to contain no DC components
options.B: General-purpose socket-outlet circuits rated up to 32 A in a dwelling
options.C: Circuits in medical locations, where continuity of supply is critical
options.D: Socket-outlets incorporating RCD protection (SRCDs) to BS 7288

questions.explanation: Regulation 531.3.3 restricts Type AC RCDs to fixed equipment whose load current is known to be free of DC components, since a DC component can impair the operation of this type. That restriction excludes socket-outlets with integral Type AC protection, and Type AC devices are also barred from medical locations.

A.text: Regulation 531.3.3 restricts Type AC RCDs to fixed equipment whose load current is known to be free of DC components, since a DC component can impair the operation of this type. That restriction excludes socket-outlets with integral Type AC protection, and Type AC devices are also barred from medical locations.

B.text: Whatever is plugged into a socket-outlet is unknown and may draw current with a DC component, so the load cannot be treated as fixed equipment with a known waveform.

C.text: Type AC devices are expressly not permitted in medical locations, regardless of what equipment is connected to the circuit.

D.text: The restriction to fixed equipment rules out Type AC protection built into a socket-outlet; SRCDs to BS 7288 are recognised only as Type A.

questions.prompt: Steel trunking passes through a wall that has a specified fire-resistance rating. Above what internal cross-sectional area must the trunking be sealed internally where it passes through the wall?
questions.explanation: Regulation 527.2.3 requires conduit, trunking or busbar trunking that penetrates a fire-resisting building element to be sealed internally once its internal cross-sectional area exceeds 710 mm², roughly a round hole 30 mm in diameter. The internal seal stops the containment acting as a path for flame and smoke through the wall.

A.text: An area of 310 mm² is roughly a 20 mm round bore, well under the size at which internal sealing of containment becomes compulsory.

B.text: At 510 mm², about a 25 mm round hole, the containment is still some 200 mm² short of the size that triggers the internal sealing requirement.

C.text: Regulation 527.2.3 requires conduit, trunking or busbar trunking that penetrates a fire-resisting building element to be sealed internally once its internal cross-sectional area exceeds 710 mm², roughly a round hole 30 mm in diameter. The internal seal stops the containment acting as a path for flame and smoke through the wall.

D.text: Waiting until the bore reaches 910 mm² would leave containment between 710 mm² and that figure unsealed, which Regulation 527.2.3 does not allow.

questions.prompt: An Electrical Installation Certificate for a new domestic (household) installation is issued complete with the Guidance for Recipients. Which notice may be omitted from the installation because its information is recorded in that certification?

options.A: The label at earthing and bonding connections
options.B: The notice advising six-monthly operation of the RCD test button
options.C: The multiple-supplies notice where an alternative supply is installed
options.D: The notice listing circuits with high protective conductor currents

questions.explanation: For domestic (household) premises, the instruction notices covering user testing of RCDs and AFDDs, the presence of SPDs and future re-inspection need not be displayed, provided the information is recorded in the initial verification certification together with the Guidance for Recipients. Warning notices for earthing and bonding connections, alternative supplies and high protective conductor currents enjoy no such relaxation and must still be fitted.

A.text: Earthing and bonding connection labels are warning notices outside the domestic relaxation; they must stay at the point of connection, though a BS 951 clamp can carry the wording.

B.text: For domestic (household) premises, the instruction notices covering user testing of RCDs and AFDDs, the presence of SPDs and future re-inspection need not be displayed, provided the information is recorded in the initial verification certification together with the Guidance for Recipients. Warning notices for earthing and bonding connections, alternative supplies and high protective conductor currents enjoy no such relaxation and must still be fitted.

C.text: Wherever an alternative or additional supply exists, the multiple-supplies warning must be displayed at the mains position, isolation points and distribution boards, dwellings included.

D.text: Circuits with high protective conductor current must always be identified at the relevant distribution board; paperwork handed to the householder does not replace that warning.

questions.prompt: A permanent label to BS 951 should be fixed in a visible position at points of connection to every earth electrode or bonding position. The wording on the label should state:

options.A: Safety Earth Connection - Do Not Remove
options.B: Safety Earth Point - Do Not Remove
options.C: Safety Earthing Connection - Do Not Remove
options.D: Safety Electrical Connection - Do Not Remove

questions.explanation: This exact phrase is required by BS 951 to warn that the connection is essential for safety and must not be tampered with. Altering or removing earth or bonding conductors can create severe electric shock risks. The wording must be uniform for legal clarity.

A.text: This conveys a similar warning but is not the prescribed BS 951 wording. The standard phrase uses 'Electrical', allowing the same label to identify both earthing and protective-bonding safety connections.

B.text: The label protects a safety connection, not merely a physical point. It also needs to cover bonding terminations that may not be an earth-electrode point.

C.text: 'Earthing' is not the specified word. The prescribed durable notice reads 'Safety Electrical Connection - Do Not Remove'.

D.text: This exact phrase is required by BS 951 to warn that the connection is essential for safety and must not be tampered with. Altering or removing earth or bonding conductors can create severe electric shock risks. The wording must be uniform for legal clarity.

questions.prompt: A low-resistance ohmmeter used for continuity verification should have what open-circuit voltage and test current?

options.A: Voltage between 0 V and 20 V; test current of at least 1 mA
options.B: Voltage between 0 V and 24 V; test current of at least 100 mA
options.C: Voltage between 4 V and 20 V; test current of at least 1 mA
options.D: Voltage between 4 V and 24 V; test current of at least 200 mA

questions.explanation: The continuity instrument should have an open-circuit voltage between 4 V and 24 V and deliver at least 200 mA at the specified low resistance. This helps reveal poor connections that a tiny signal current might not expose.

A.text: The voltage range incorrectly permits no effective test voltage, while the stated current is far too small for protective-conductor continuity verification. A substantial test current is needed to expose resistive joints reliably.

B.text: Although the upper voltage is plausible, the range still starts below the specified minimum and the current is only half the required level. Both instrument characteristics must meet the continuity-test recommendation.

C.text: The lower voltage boundary is suitable, but the current corresponds to insulation-tester capability rather than low-resistance continuity testing. It may fail to reveal a poor connection that behaves differently under a meaningful test current.

D.text: The continuity instrument should have an open-circuit voltage between 4 V and 24 V and deliver at least 200 mA at the specified low resistance. This helps reveal poor connections that a tiny signal current might not expose.

questions.prompt: An RCD is to be tested by applying a residual test current between line and the cpc on the load side of the device. Why is it essential that the earth fault loop impedance of the circuit is verified before this test is made?

options.A: The RCD tester cannot select its test current until the measured Zs has been entered
options.B: The test can put a dangerous voltage on exposed-conductive-parts if Zs is near its limit
options.C: The measured Zs is used to calculate the maximum operating time the RCD must achieve
options.D: The loop impedance reading confirms that the RCD's breaking capacity exceeds the fault current

questions.explanation: The tester drives a residual current through the line conductor and the protective conductor, so a voltage appears across the earth return path in proportion to its impedance. Where Zs is close to the maximum acceptable value, that voltage on exposed- and extraneous-conductive-parts can be dangerous to anyone touching them. Confirming the loop impedance first shows the earth path is sound before current is deliberately passed through it.

A.text: RCD test currents are set on the instrument from the device's rated IΔn and Type; no loop impedance value is entered in order to set them.

B.text: The tester drives a residual current through the line conductor and the protective conductor, so a voltage appears across the earth return path in proportion to its impedance. Where Zs is close to the maximum acceptable value, that voltage on exposed- and extraneous-conductive-parts can be dangerous to anyone touching them. Confirming the loop impedance first shows the earth path is sound before current is deliberately passed through it.

C.text: Maximum expected tripping times are fixed by the device standard and the residual current applied, for example 300 ms at 1 × IΔn for a non-delay device to a harmonised standard, and are not derived from the measured Zs.

D.text: Breaking capacity is compared with prospective fault current, which is a separate check and not the safety reason for measuring loop impedance ahead of an RCD test.

questions.prompt: Regulation 643.1 requires a group of tests to be carried out in a set order before a new installation is energised. Which of the following lists only tests that belong to that group?

options.A: Continuity of protective conductors, continuity of ring final circuit conductors, insulation resistance and polarity
options.B: Continuity of protective conductors, insulation resistance, earth fault loop impedance and prospective fault current
options.C: Insulation resistance, polarity, check of phase sequence and functional testing
options.D: Continuity of ring final circuit conductors, insulation resistance, operation of RCDs and verification of voltage drop

questions.explanation: Regulation 643.1 places the tests of Regulations 643.2 to 643.6 before energisation: continuity of protective conductors and ring final circuits, insulation resistance, SELV, PELV or electrical separation, insulation of non-conducting floors and walls, and polarity. These dead tests prove the installation is safe to make live. Any unsatisfactory result should be put right before moving on to the next test.

A.text: Regulation 643.1 places the tests of Regulations 643.2 to 643.6 before energisation: continuity of protective conductors and ring final circuits, insulation resistance, SELV, PELV or electrical separation, insulation of non-conducting floors and walls, and polarity. These dead tests prove the installation is safe to make live. Any unsatisfactory result should be put right before moving on to the next test.

B.text: Earth fault loop impedance (Regulation 643.7.3) and prospective fault current (Regulation 643.7.3.201) belong to the automatic disconnection group that follows polarity, outside Regulations 643.2 to 643.6.

C.text: Phase sequence is checked under Regulation 643.9 and functional testing under Regulation 643.10, both near the end of the sequence and well after the group that must precede energisation.

D.text: RCD operation and verification of voltage drop (Regulation 643.11) sit after the pre-energisation group; an RCD cannot be trip-tested without a supply.

questions.prompt: Before connecting an RCD tester on a TT installation, the inspector presses the integral test button on the RCD and the device trips. What does this result tell the inspector about the installation's earthing?

options.A: The earth electrode resistance is low enough for the RCD to operate at IΔn
options.B: The earthing conductor is continuous, although the circuit cpcs remain unproven

questions.prompt: What is the status of the 5 × IΔn test on a 30 mA RCD under BS 7671:2018+A2:2022, as explained in Guidance Note 3?

questions.explanation: The test that BS 7671:2018+A2:2022 requires is the one at 1 × IΔn, while the 5 × IΔn test is listed among optional tests for fault-finding and similar purposes. questions.prompt: According to Guidance Note 3, how should an installation be arranged when the external earth fault loop impedance (Ze) is measured at the origin with an earth fault loop impedance tester?

questions.explanation: Ze is measured between the incoming line conductor and the means of earthing with the main switch open, or with all circuits isolated. questions.prompt: A minor works certificate shall be issued where?

options.A: An additional circuit is connected to an installation
options.B: An alteration not requiring an additional circuit is needed
options.C: The property current demand is to be increased
options.D: Work is carried out in a domestic situation only

questions.explanation: A Minor Electrical Installation Works Certificate is used when an existing circuit is altered or extended, but no new circuit is added. Examples include adding a socket to an existing ring or changing a light fitting and its associated wiring. When a new circuit is installed, a full Electrical Installation Certificate is required instead. The certificate applies to all types of premises, not just domestic ones.

A.text: The model minor-works form expressly excludes the provision of a new circuit. A new circuit needs an Electrical Installation Certificate and the applicable schedules.

B.text: A Minor Electrical Installation Works Certificate is used when an existing circuit is altered or extended, but no new circuit is added. C.text: A demand change is a design consideration, not a certificate category. The correct form depends on the extent of the physical installation work, especially whether a new circuit is provided.

D.text: The form is not restricted to dwellings. It can document a qualifying small addition or alteration in any installation within its stated scope.

questions.prompt: As defined in Part 2 of BS 7671, what is a 'departure'?

options.A: A deliberate decision not to comply fully, which the designer declares to be no less safe

questions.explanation: A departure is intentional: the designer chooses not to follow a requirement of BS 7671 fully and must declare that the resulting degree of safety is not less than full compliance would achieve. It is therefore a conscious, justified design choice and not an oversight or a fault discovered afterwards.

questions.prompt: A new single-phase installation is ready for initial verification. questions.explanation: Each test makes the next one safe. Insulation resistance shows there is no short circuit or earth fault, and polarity then confirms that fuses and single-pole devices are in the line conductor; Regulation 643.1 requires both before energising. With the supply on, Zs is measured before the RCDs are tested, because an RCD test deliberately passes current to earth and the earth path must already be proven. Functional testing follows once the protective measures are known to work.
